opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've gone back and forth on. The intuition is really seductive: AlphaGo showed that if you pair a learned policy and value function with search, you get something much stronger than either alone. So people naturally ask why we can't just do that for reasoning: treat each token, or each step of a chain of thought, as a move, and search over the tree.

I think the honest answer is that the analogy breaks in a few important places.

The first is the branching factor and what a "move" even is. In Go you have a few hundred legal moves and a crisp game state. In language, the action space is the whole vocabulary at every token, and most of the branching is semantically meaningless. "Therefore" versus "thus" isn't a meaningful fork. So you have to search at the level of ideas or reasoning steps, and then you need to define what a step is, which is itself fuzzy.

The second, and to me the bigger one, is the value function. Go has a perfect simulator and an unambiguous terminal reward: you win or you lose. MCTS works because rollouts and the value network are grounded in that. For open-ended reasoning, you usually don't have a reliable verifier for intermediate states. If your value model is miscalibrated, search just finds adversarial paths that fool it. You're optimizing against your own critic, and that tends to go badly.

Where it does make sense is in domains that look more like Go: math with formal proof checkers, code with unit tests, anything where you can verify cheaply. There, search plus a learned prior is genuinely powerful.

But what's been striking is that a lot of the gains people hoped to get from explicit tree search seem to come from just training the model with RL to do the search implicitly, in its own chain of thought. The model learns to backtrack, try alternatives, check its work, all inside one linear sequence. That's kind of a bitter-lesson result: rather than hand-engineering the search structure, you let the network internalize it, and it amortizes the search into the policy.

So I'd say MCTS isn't wrong as a mental model; distillation of search into the policy is exactly what AlphaZero did too. It's just that for language, the explicit tree is probably less important than having good verifiers and letting RL teach the model to search on its own.

r002.rationale: It says Go has a value network grounded in a simulator and terminal reward, but does not explain that the value function can evaluate a trajectory without completing it.

r003.rationale: It mentions distilling search into a policy, but does not explain how local MCTS results in Go become targets for iterative policy improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that it's a lot less clean than the AlphaGo analogy makes it sound, and I say that as someone who's pretty bullish on search in general.

The reason MCTS worked so beautifully for Go is that you had three things lined up. You had a perfect simulator, so you could roll out a position and know exactly what the board looks like afterward. You had a terminal reward that was unambiguous, you win or you lose. And you had a relatively small, discrete action space at each step. Language reasoning breaks all three of those at once. There's no simulator for "what does the world look like after I assert this intermediate step," the reward is mostly only available on a narrow set of tasks like math and code where you can actually check the answer, and the branching factor at the token level is just enormous.

So the naive version, where you literally do tree search over tokens with a value head, I think is mostly a dead end. People tried it and it's compute-hungry and the value estimates are too noisy to steer the tree well.

What I think actually works, and what I suspect is going on inside the reasoning models we've seen, is something that rhymes with MCTS but at a much coarser granularity. You search over thoughts or sub-plans rather than tokens. You use the model itself as the rollout policy and as a soft verifier. And crucially, most of the "search" ends up getting amortized back into the weights through training, which is the real lesson of AlphaZero anyway. The tree search at inference time was never the product. The product was the policy that got distilled from it.

The other thing I'd push on is that the environments where this is tractable right now, math, code, formal proofs, those are exactly the Go-like environments where you do have a verifier. So you get this uneven progress where models get superhuman at competition math and still can't reliably plan a dinner party. Closing that gap is really a question of whether you can build good enough learned verifiers for fuzzy domains, and I think that's more of an open problem than people admit. My guess is the answer is yes eventually, but it looks a lot more like RL with a learned reward model than it looks like a tree.

r001.rationale: The response says search can be amortized into model weights through training, but does not explain that successful trajectories reinforce tokens regardless of whether those tokens contributed to the correct answer.

r002.rationale: It mentions noisy value estimates and a perfect Go simulator, but does not explain that a value function can evaluate a trajectory without unfolding it to completion.

r003.rationale: It says AlphaZero's policy was distilled from tree search, but does not explain that local Go MCTS results serve as targets for iterative policy improvement.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic about search, but I don’t think you can take the AlphaGo recipe and apply it directly to language. In Go, you have a precisely defined state, a finite set of legal moves, and an unambiguous outcome. With language, even deciding what constitutes a move is tricky. Is it a token, a sentence, or an entire reasoning step?

The bigger issue is evaluation. If you generate ten different arguments, how do you know which one is taking you somewhere useful? A model can be very confident about a plausible but incorrect argument. Searching harder against that evaluator might just find more convincing mistakes.

Coding is a promising setting because you can execute the program and get feedback. Math can have that property when you have a formal verifier. There, search has something solid to push against, although verifying a final answer doesn’t automatically tell you how to score a partial solution.

So I’d distinguish the broad idea of spending more computation at inference time from Monte Carlo tree search specifically. I’m bullish on generating alternatives, testing them, and revising. Whether a tree is the right structure, or whether you want something closer to iterative refinement, probably depends on the task. The important thing is having feedback that lets extra computation translate into better answers.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses uncertainty in scoring arguments and the risk of confident errors, but does not say that rewarding a successful trajectory reinforces all its tokens regardless of their contribution.

r002.rationale: It contrasts language-model evaluation with Go’s clear outcomes, but does not explain how a value function can score a trajectory before it is unfolded to completion.

r003.rationale: It does not describe Go MCTS results as targets for iteratively improving the policy; its discussion of testing and revising is general.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what’s the equivalent of the simulator? In Go, you know the legal moves, you can cheaply advance the board state, and at the end you know who won. You can search a lot without having to ask whether the rules of the game are correct.

For language-model reasoning, you can certainly generate a tree of possible next steps. But how do you decide which branch is better? If you’re asking another language model to judge, it may have the same blind spots as the model generating the answers. Search can end up amplifying the evaluator’s mistakes.

That makes me more optimistic about domains where you have an external check—code you can execute, for example. There, spending more computation exploring alternatives has a clear mechanism for improving the answer. For an open-ended question, it’s much less obvious what the reward should be.

So I think there’s a lot of promise in inference-time search, but I wouldn’t assume the right implementation is literally the Go algorithm. You might want to explore several approaches, run experiments, backtrack, and use the results to decide what to try next. The important thing is having feedback that actually tells you you’re making progress.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Go’s cheap state transitions and known outcome with language-model evaluation, but does not explain how a value function can score a trajectory before it is unfolded to completion.

r003.rationale: It discusses search and experimenting with alternatives, but does not describe using local Go MCTS results as targets for iterative policy improvement.
